title: Node lease leak caused by lease controller swallowing error
body:
### What happened?

Hello,

We have a cluster that's showing a constant increase in node lease objects. One particularity of the leaked leases is that  they don't have an OwnerReference.

Looking at the code, the ownerReference is set by this kubelet function [`SetNodeOwnerFunc`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/dad95e1be65d4e74d33c810f4395596a22115717/pkg/kubelet/util/nodelease.go#L32) which is called by the lease controller in [`newLease`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/dad95e1be65d4e74d33c810f4395596a22115717/staging/src/k8s.io/component-helpers/apimachinery/lease/controller.go#L230-L233). 

Note that  `newLease` returns `lease` even if the call to `newLeasePostProcessFunc` fails. The means `lease` is returned despite being potentially without an ownerRef.

Looking at `newLease()` call site in [`retryUpdateLease`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/dad95e1be65d4e74d33c810f4395596a22115717/staging/src/k8s.io/component-helpers/apimachinery/lease/controller.go#L187) we see that the returned error is swallowed meaning the controller will make calls to `c.leaseClient.Update` with an incomplete lease.

We don't have access to the worker nodes or the kubelet logs but this explanation match what we are seeing when looking at the audit logs where the call which creates the lease without ownerRef is an Update call.


### What did you expect to happen?

Node lease should always be created with an ownerRef

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

To repro, setup a cluster with a worker node, delete the worker node object (but keep the node+kubelet running):
```
kubectl delete no ip-192-168-212-28.us-west-2.compute.internal
```
Then look at the lease, the original one will be removed by the GC but kubelet will eventually re-create it without an ownerRef:
```
$ kubectl -n kube-node-lease get lease ip-192-168-212-28.us-west-2.compute.internal -o json
{
    "apiVersion": "coordination.k8s.io/v1",
    "kind": "Lease",
    "metadata": {
        "creationTimestamp": "2023-07-28T21:05:05Z",
        "name": "ip-192-168-212-28.us-west-2.compute.internal",
        "namespace": "kube-node-lease",
        "resourceVersion": "1942799",
        "uid": "86429d42-7508-4929-84b2-1435ea3c6d71"
    },
    "spec": {
        "holderIdentity": "ip-192-168-212-28.us-west-2.compute.internal",
        "leaseDurationSeconds": 40,
        "renewTime": "2023-07-28T21:06:27.474137Z"
    }
}
```

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

title: Api server does not start
body:

After a blackout, when I restarted the cluster (2 Controllers + 3 Workers), none of the Control-Plane nodes started the api-server, neither kube-controller-manager, kube-scheduler and etcd pods. The port 6443 is not opened. 
No changes were made in the previous week.

body:

```go

	"os"

}

title: Job: Pod backoff calculation should not depend on failure policy
body:
### What happened?

Pod backoff calculation excludes pods that match an `Ignore` rule in the failure policy:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/847f1758748ac357e79094c5e85029a10428e65f/pkg/controller/job/job_controller.go#L1365

This could lead to fast retries, overwhelming the control plane, if most failures match an `Ignore` rule. The semantics of `Ignore` is not to count towards the limit, but the backoff should still be respected.

/sig apps

### What did you expect to happen?

Recreations to be throttled.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create a Job with failure policy that matches every kind of failure.
1. Use a container that always fails

You would observe immediate recreation.

The call stack is showing client-go version 0.26.0, but there was a problem in client-go versions 0.26.0-0.26.3 related to aggregated discovery which was promoted to beta (enabled by default) in k8s version 1.27.  The comment I linked says the problem was fixed in client-go version 0.26.4

title: Repeated server side apply to a statefulset updates the revisionVersion, even without template modifications.
body:
### What happened?

I am utilizing server-side apply to generate a statefulset using the provided template. Afterwards, without modifying the template, I perform server-side apply once more with the expectation that it will not alter the statefulset in any manner. However, I have observed that server-side apply does update the resourceVersion and managedFields time, but otherwise no changes. Each subsequent apply operation also updates the resourceVersion and managedFields time.

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: test-ssa
  labels:
    app: test-ssa
spec:
  serviceName: "test-ssa"
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: test-ssa
  replicas: 1
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: test-ssa
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: test-ssa
          image: alpine:3.17.4
          command: ["sh", "-c", "while true; do echo 'sleep 10'; sleep 10; done"]
          volumeMounts:
          - name: pvc
            mountPath: /etc
          resources:
            limits:
              cpu: "2"
              ephemeral-storage: 1Gi
              memory: 2Gi
            requests:
              cpu: 100m
              ephemeral-storage: 1Gi
              memory: 128Mi
  volumeClaimTemplates:
    - apiVersion: v1
      kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
      metadata:
        name: pvc
      spec:
        accessModes: [ "ReadWriteOnce" ]
        resources:
          requests:
            storage: 1Gi
        storageClassName: rbd-ssd
```

I've also observed that if I modify `volumeClaimTemplates` section by adding some extra fields(shown below) generated by the k8s then server side apply does NOT update resourceVersion. 
```diff
...
  volumeClaimTemplates:
    - apiVersion: v1
      kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
      metadata:
+       creationTimestamp: null
        name: pvc
      spec:
        accessModes: [ "ReadWriteOnce" ]
        resources:
          requests:
            storage: 1Gi
        storageClassName: rbd-ssd
+       volumeMode: Filesystem
+     status:
+       phase: Pending
```

Can anyone please explain this behavior? I haven't observed similar behavior while testing with other resource types, statefulset seems to be somewhat special. 

UPDATE1: I've found that this has already been reported in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/95460 however it looks like the issue is still not resolved.

UPDATE2: This issue can also be reproduced when environment variables are used to expose Pod fields like shown below:
```yaml
...
env:
  - name: "NODE_NAME"
    valueFrom:
      fieldRef:
        apiVersion: "v1"
        fieldPath: "spec.nodeName"
...
```
if the `apiVersion: "v1"` field is omitted then server-side apply will update resourceVersion.

### What did you expect to happen?

I expected that performing repeated server-side apply without any template modifications would not update the resourceVersion.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

`test-ssa.yaml`

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: test-ssa
  labels:
    app: test-ssa
spec:
  serviceName: "test-ssa"
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: test-ssa
  replicas: 1
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: test-ssa
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: test-ssa
          image: alpine:3.17.4
          command: ["sh", "-c", "while true; do echo 'sleep 10'; sleep 10; done"]
          volumeMounts:
          - name: pvc
            mountPath: /etc
          resources:
            limits:
              cpu: "2"
              ephemeral-storage: 1Gi
              memory: 2Gi
            requests:
              cpu: 100m
              ephemeral-storage: 1Gi
              memory: 128Mi
  volumeClaimTemplates:
    - apiVersion: v1
      kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
      metadata:
        name: pvc
      spec:
        accessModes: [ "ReadWriteOnce" ]
        resources:
          requests:
            storage: 1Gi
        storageClassName: rbd-ssd
```
You can see that every time you run the command shown below resourceVersion of the `test-ssa` statefulset is updated.
`k apply -f test-ssa.yaml --server-side=true --field-manager=test --force-conflicts=true`

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

title: Default load balancing when using NodePort services
body:
### What happened?

/sig network
/kind support

I am trying to understand how Kubernetes does load balancing when using NodePort services (I am explicitely not referring to cloud provider load balancers). I created the following setup:

- 5 worker nodes ( `worker1`, `worker2`, `worker3`, `worker4`, `worker5` )
- 1 master node ( `master` )

I created a deployment with 5 replica pods, scheduled in a way that each of the worker nodes hosts 1 pod. I use a NodePort service (port `30500`) to expose the pods for external requests. I now send requests from an external device to the master node ( `master:30500` )

### What did you expect to happen?

From the [source code](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0ae9aaacfa217b18652f34d6ef29f08a15851b0a/pkg/proxy/ipvs/proxier.go#L87) and other websites, I expected round-robin load balancing. 

I tested different load intensities (requests per second). The result was always the same: the pod that processes the request seemed to be selected randomly.  My question is why and is it intended behavior?

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

To reproduce just use any kind of container that is able to process load requests, deploy multiple replicas on different nodes and send requests from an external device.

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

### Kubernetes version

<details>
Kubernetes version v1.27.2

None, bare-metal

title: Yaml file using autoscaling/v1 creates an HPA with autoscaling/v2
body:
### What happened?

Using this yaml file:
```
apiVersion: autoscaling/v1
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: example-autoscaler
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: example-deployment
  minReplicas: 2
  maxReplicas: 10
  targetCPUUtilizationPercentage: 70
```
And then running `kubectl create -f <yaml_file>`, I ended up with a `autoscaling/v2` HPA:
```
17:17:39 > $ kubectl get hpa/example-autoscaler -o yaml
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: example-autoscaler
  namespace: default
spec:
  maxReplicas: 10
  metrics:
  - resource:
      name: cpu
      target:
        averageUtilization: 70
        type: Utilization
    type: Resource
  minReplicas: 2
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: example-deployment
...
```

### What did you expect to happen?

Was expecting the HPA to be created with api version `autoscaling/v1`. Is this expected behavior? I can't find it from the documentation

/sig autoscaling

/kind support

Here's an analogy: you telephone the booking office for a railway and book a seat on a train. You call the old number and get through to the old booking office, who are following an established procedure.

Later, you have your assistant (`kubectl`) check with the railway about your reservation. Your assistant calls the current booking office on the recommended number. The booking office confirm your booking, but give slightly different information about the trip.

If you enquire carefully at the booking office, you can learn that you created the booking by contacting the old booking office. However this information isn't relevant to the enquiries team and they have to check specially to find out. In a normal enquiry, people just want to know about their seat, carriage, direction of travel etc.

When you ask `kubectl` to fetch the HPA, kubectl uses the best available API version to do that. However, the HPA is the **same object** whether you fetch it using the v1 API (analogous to telephoning the old number), or the v2 API.

Another similar explanation I wrote a while ago: https://serverfault.com/a/1104587

There's nothing to fix.

That's fair, thanks. I agree no fix needed. The closest explanation seems to be from the link shared (https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/kubernetes-api/#api-groups-and-versioning):

> The API server handles the conversion between API versions transparently: all the different versions are actually representations of the same persisted data. The API server may serve the same underlying data through multiple API versions. 

> If you originally created an object using the v1beta1 version of its API, you can later read, update, or delete that object using either the v1beta1 or the v1 API version

Although they refer to the same object, it was written in a certain version but results of fetching/reading it resulted with another. It's like ordering a paperback, but getting a hardbound instead (though it's the same book and the author recommends the hardbound). It's a bit of surprising behaviour but I guess a pleasant one

title: NodeLocalDNS not working with custom hosts
body:
### What happened?

In EKS 1.22, after installing nodelocaldns, in-cluster DNS and external DNS works normally, but custom hosts stored in coredns configmap, stop working.

### What did you expect to happen?

I expect that even with nodelocaldns, custom hosts continue to work normally.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Configure custom hosts in coredns configmap

```
# kubectl edit configmap coredns -n kube-system

hosts custom.hosts mydns.rtm {
        8.8.4.4 mydns.rtm
        fallthrough
       }

```

2. Ping mydns.rtm

```
# kubectl exec -it nginx2-55764b6d95-dvvdh -- ping mydns.rtm
PING mydns.rtm (8.8.4.4): 56 data bytes

#!/bin/sh

echo "Downloading nodelocaldns"
wget https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/v1.22.17/cluster/addons/dns/nodelocaldns/nodelocaldns.yaml -O manifests/nodelocaldns.yaml

sed -i '' -e 's/__PILLAR__DNS__SERVER__/172.20.0.10/g' manifests/nodelocaldns.yaml ### kubectl -n kube-system get service kube-dns

nodes.body: /sig node

This issue appears to be related to the creation of an ephemeral container using a restricted debugging profile within a restricted PodSecurity (PS) namespace. The user attempted to create the ephemeral container using the kubectl debug command with specific parameters, but encountered an error.

The error message indicates that the pod "ephemeral-demo-b78475778-hmpl7" violates the PodSecurity policy named "restricted:latest" due to several conditions not being met. The error message lists the specific violations:

    allowPrivilegeEscalation is not set to false for the containers.
    The containers have unrestricted capabilities and must set securityContext.capabilities.drop to ["ALL"].
    The containers include "NET_ADMIN" and "SYS_PTRACE" in securityContext.capabilities.add, which is not allowed.
    runAsNonRoot is not set to true for the pod or containers.
    seccompProfile is not set to "RuntimeDefault" or "Localhost" for the pod or containers.

These violations prevent the creation of the ephemeral container using the restricted debugging profile. The purpose of the restricted debugging profile is to provide a more secure environment for debugging, but in this case, the restrictions specified in the PodSecurity policy are not being met.

Right.

I shall be able to create ephemeral container with restricted debugging profile under a restricted PS namespace successfully.

title: Metadata of immutable secrets cannot be changed when the `.data` has a key with empty value
body:
### What happened?

I have created the following secret in my cluster.

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: test
immutable: true
data:
  "foo": ""
  "one": dHdvCg==
```

When I add labels to my secret and try to apply it in the cluster I get the following error 
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: test
  labels:
    "foo": "bar"
immutable: true
data:
  "foo": ""
  "one": dHdvCg==

```

$ k apply -f secret.yaml
The Secret "test" is invalid: data: Forbidden: field is immutable when `immutable` is set

Not sure why, but `kubectl label` works.

title: Running pods with devices are terminated if kubelet is restarted
body:
### What happened?

In KubeVirt project, we now see a regression when running on Kubernetes `1.25.10 | 1.26.5 | 1.27.2`. If kubelet is restarted on a node, then all the existing and running workloads that use devices are terminated with `UnexpectedAdmissionError`:
```
Warning  UnexpectedAdmissionError  45s   kubelet            Allocate failed due to no healthy devices present; cannot allocate unhealthy devices devices.kubevirt.io/kvm, which is unexpected
Normal   Killing                   42s   kubelet            Stopping container compute
```
KubeVirt runs virtual machines inside pods and uses a device plugin to advertise e.g. `/dev/kvm` on the nodes.

Presumably, this PR changed the behavior: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/116376
Original issue: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/109595

### What did you expect to happen?

A potential restart of kubelet should not interrupt the running workloads.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?
with KubeVirt:

- run a KubeVirt VM
- `pkill kubelet`
- observe that the workload pod gets terminated

or with https://github.com/k8stopologyawareschedwg/sample-device-plugin

- make deploy
- make test-both
- pkill kubelet
- the pod gets restarted

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

### Kubernetes version

<details>

This affects the 1.25.x, 1.26.x and 1.27.x branches.

1.25.10 | 1.26.5 | 1.27.2

</details>

I was also able to reproduce it without KubeVirt. I used https://github.com/k8stopologyawareschedwg/sample-device-plugin

The steps are:
- `make deploy`
- `make test-both`
- `pkill kubelet`
```
Warning  UnexpectedAdmissionError  30s   kubelet            Allocate failed due to no healthy devices present; cannot allocate unhealthy devices example.com/deviceA, which is unexpected
```

My observation is that the original issue https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/109595 was focused on the node reboot scenario. Then the PR https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/116376 fixed that. But in the case when only kubelet is restarted and some workloads are still running, there is the problem that device plugins may take time to initialize and report back healthy devices. Meanwhile, kubelet terminates the running pods as it assumes an unexpected admission.
/sig node

/triage accepted

we have reproducers
/cc

I'm looking into this issue and I'll be updating shortly. At this point in time I can say that yes, https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/116376 made the devicemanager stricter and leads to this behavior. We may need another way to fix the inconsistency reported in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/109595 , and likely we will need to tight up/fix the e2e tests about device plugins.

But there could be a (partially?) mismatched expectation as well, because AFAIK the [kubelet will run admission on restart (and in general on initialization)](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go#L2409C3-L2413) and thus may kill running pods.

In other words, **in addition** to the followup fix, it would be beneficial to clarify that in general running containers are or are not guaranteed to survive a kubelet restart.

> In other words, in addition to the followup fix, it would be beneficial to clarify that in general running containers are or are not guaranteed to survive a kubelet restart.

From the user point of view, I guess, kubelet should keep the running pods. Kubelet can be restarted for various reasons, but IMHO it should not affect critical workloads. Hm... I thought that it was actually the supposed behavior to always try to keep the pods.

> > In other words, in addition to the followup fix, it would be beneficial to clarify that in general running containers are or are not guaranteed to survive a kubelet restart.
> 
> From the user point of view, I guess, kubelet should keep the running pods. Kubelet can be restarted for various reasons, but IMHO it should not affect critical workloads. Hm... I thought that it was actually the supposed behavior to always try to keep the pods.

I agree this is a desirable and expected behavior, if nothing else out of habit. This is what kubelet implementation did.

However, the deeper I look, the less I'm sure it is a _guaranteed_ behavior.

There are well known circumnstances on which kubelet may reserve the option to kill running pods when kubelet restarts, e.g. if the machine config changes. Granted, this is NOT the case which is reported here (nothing changed across restart, hence we want a followup fix of some kind), but I'm convinced that clarifying the guarantees on kubelet restart should be part of the ongoing conversation.

Important to note in this discussion, and regraldess of how the kubelet should behave: Please recognize the fact that kubelte behaved like this for many years, and there might be a few projects out there who assume htis behavior.

Again: I#m not judging if it's right or wrong, but only about that we "break userspace" - if this would be the kernel. And just like the kernel, we should avoid these things.
/cc
/cc
/cc

/priority critical-urgent

it's true [we changed a long-established behavior](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/118559#issuecomment-1582447055), so let's find a consensus quickly about the resolution.
I want to help with a followup change, and I'd rather have the project **not** to chose between this regression and regressing over https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/109595 (still very much real) so I'll be posting a POC to accomodate both needs shortly.

/cc @klueska (device manager) @SergeyKanzhelev @mrunalp @dchen1107 @derekwaynecarr (sig-node)

1. Running pods should always survive kubelet restart.
2. Admission is re-run on every kubelet restart (it must, because the kubelet is stateless and we have coupled admission with allocation)
3. It is the responsibility of every admission plugin to handle the scenario of kubelet restart correctly (by identifying when it can start making admission decisions)
4. We probably lack all the tools to correctly handle admission + allocation, and we need to identify which ones to add.
5. Admission is processed in a serial (and mostly random) order and therefore admission plugins cannot safely "block" until initialization is complete

It sounds like this is because the device admission plugin is still not able to authoritatively state whether a device is available at the time the restarted pod is run?  

We need to make some changes to admission generally to solve this case completely, but until we do, is it possible to have the admission plugin safely accept a pod that is a) never before seen by the device plugin and b) in the running phase?  Or are there other reasons why that has been tried and found not to work?

Thanks Clayton for chiming in.

> 1. Running pods should always survive kubelet restart.
> 
>     2. Admission is re-run on every kubelet restart (it must, because the kubelet is stateless and we have coupled admission with allocation)
> 
>     3. It is the responsibility of every admission plugin to handle the scenario of kubelet restart correctly (by identifying when it can start making admission decisions)
> 
>     4. We probably lack all the tools to correctly handle admission + allocation, and we need to identify which ones to add.
> 
>     5. Admission is processed in a serial (and mostly random) order and therefore admission plugins cannot safely "block" until initialization is complete
> 
> 
> It sounds like this is because the device admission plugin is still not able to authoritatively state whether a device is available at the time the restarted pod is run?

The device manager is invoked as part of admission and it performs allocation. Up until the device plugins register themselves, the device manager cannot indeed provide authoritative answers about device availability. Any answer is essentially wrong at this stage. For context, the current behaviour loudly breaks all the pods on restart, the previous silently broke some pods.

> We need to make some changes to admission generally to solve this case completely, but until we do, is it possible to have the admission plugin safely accept a pod that is a) never before seen by the device plugin and b) in the running phase? Or are there other reasons why that has been tried and found not to work?

This is one of the option I'm evaluating. I'm willing to explore this path, my concern is that will require the device manager to gain knowledge about running pods, asking the pod cache or the kuberuntime. If this is acceptable designwise I'll start to sketch an implementation we can iterate upon.

I have another POC which is about letting the kubelet wait (up until a timeout) for device plugins to register themselves before start syncing pods, I'll upload it for reference very shortly.

> my concern is that will require the device manager to gain knowledge about running pods, asking the pod cache or the kuberuntime

At admission time on a restart you won't actually know whether the pod is running, because the kubelet itself won't know, because admission on restart is the transition from "unknown state" to "should still be running".  And the kubelet implemention is very naive - we assume admission is fast, reentrant, and cheap, none of which are completely true with the more complex admission requirements of cpu manager, device manager, etc.  

I *think* asking pod cache or kuberuntime directly would not be appropriate.  However, at admission time you *do* know what other pods have been previously admitted (passed as an argument), and you also know what pods *you've* seen.  So if you see a Running pod submitted to admission, and the device plugin internal state does not say that the pod's devices, you can treat that as "i previously admitted this" and accept it.  If that requires significant changes to device manager internal state, it might be worth discussing what other changes to device manager might make sense.

> I have another POC which is about letting the kubelet wait (up until a timeout) for device plugins to register themselves before start syncing pods, I'll upload it for reference very shortly.

This could be problematic in some cases, like starting static pods.  Do device plugins typically consult control plane resources during initialization?  For some distros, the control plane runs in static pods so that would potentially block restart in a failure scenario.  If the device plugins are *only* checking local state, and registration is fast, that might be ok.  However, in general I would say this is the wrong approach in general - we only want pods that need devices to be impacted by a slow device plugin.  That argues that we should have a "no decision" option for admission, and then we simply keep retrying via the kubelet resync loop (HandlePodCleanups, which attempts to start pods that are in config but not running).

I'm slightly leaning towards adding "no decision, retry later" option because it should work pretty cleanly and be safe to backport to at least 1.27 (we made 1.27 retry later possible, so that could be an input here).  But it would be ok to have two separate fixes - one for 1.25/1.26 and one for 1.27+.

OK, time for me to ask some silly questions because we're reaching very fast the edge of my knowledge of the kubelet outside the resource managers :)

> > my concern is that will require the device manager to gain knowledge about running pods, asking the pod cache or the kuberuntime
> 
> At admission time on a restart you won't actually know whether the pod is running, because the kubelet itself won't know, because admission on restart is the transition from "unknown state" to "should still be running". And the kubelet implemention is very naive - we assume admission is fast, reentrant, and cheap, none of which are completely true with the more complex admission requirements of cpu manager, device manager, etc.

> I _think_ asking pod cache or kuberuntime directly would not be appropriate. However, at admission time you _do_ know what other pods have been previously admitted (passed as an argument), and you also know what pods _you've_ seen. 

Thanks for pointing out, I'll play with this code a bit

> So if you see a Running pod submitted to admission, and the device plugin internal state does not say that the pod's devices, you can treat that as "i previously admitted this" and accept it. If that requires significant changes to device manager internal state, it might be worth discussing what other changes to device manager might make sense.

Just to be sure, does this mean that admission plugin can trust the pod status they receive (e.g. is it up to date)? otherwise how can detect a pod is Running?

> > I have another POC which is about letting the kubelet wait (up until a timeout) for device plugins to register themselves before start syncing pods, I'll upload it for reference very shortly.
> 
> This could be problematic in some cases, like starting static pods. Do device plugins typically consult control plane resources during initialization?

_Typically *AFAIK*_ no, but we don't know for sure.

> For some distros, the control plane runs in static pods so that would potentially block restart in a failure scenario. If the device plugins are _only_ checking local state, and registration is fast, that might be ok.

We can't however guarantee that and so it can break randomly, so I seems to me this is a dealbreaker for this approach - too fragile with known cases

> However, in general I would say this is the wrong approach in general - we only want pods that need devices to be impacted by a slow device plugin. 

I concur

> That argues that we should have a "no decision" option for admission, and then we simply keep retrying via the kubelet resync loop (HandlePodCleanups, which attempts to start pods that are in config but not running).

OK, but resource managers (device, cpu, ...) run as part of kubelet `admitHandlers` (vs `softAdmitHandlers`) and so their rejection is always final. Or there's a way to signal from these handlers "dunno, retry later" I'm missing? (xref: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.28.0-alpha.2/pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go#LL1250-L1257 and https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.28.0-alpha.2/pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go#L2572)

> I'm slightly leaning towards adding "no decision, retry later" option because it should work pretty cleanly and be safe to backport to at least 1.27 (we made 1.27 retry later possible, so that could be an input here). But it would be ok to have two separate fixes - one for 1.25/1.26 and one for 1.27+.

Assuming the retry approach turns out clean, would invasive backports to 1.26/1.25 be needed to include the prerequisite work?

Appears to me that we have two options:

1. Impart device manager the intelligence so that it maintains an internal state of the pods that were previously admitted by it and take that into consideration when running pods are re-admitted on kubelet restarts.
2.  "no decision" option for admission and retry later.

I understand Option 1 would require additional information to be passed to changes to device manager admission check and would be confined to kubelet and hence more focused at addressing this specific problem. On the other hand, Option 2 would not only help out in resolving this issue but also other broader set of issues e.g. [scheduler being topology-unaware can cause runaway pod creation]( https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/84869) which could be another reason to pursue this option in addition to backportabliity as mentioned above . 

@smarterclayton Could you please clarify a couple of questions based on your vision of the "no decision" option:

- How would we distinguish between the system being in steady state when pods are supposed to go through the admission flow as normal as opposed to cases like kubelet restart where we might want delayed/no decision admission?
- Is this going to be an opt-in capability at a pod level or a node level?

> Admission is re-run on every kubelet restart (it must, because the kubelet is stateless and we have coupled admission with allocation)

Perhaps decoupling admission and allocation could ease some of the pain here? I wonder what was the reason for coupling the two in the first place. It seems reasonable to re-admit pods on kubelet restart but I am not sure why resource allocation needs to happen again for already running pods.
/cc

> How would we distinguish between the system being in steady state when pods are supposed to go through the admission flow as normal as opposed to cases like kubelet restart where we might want delayed/no decision admission?

Once all device plugins have checked in, i think it's reasonable for the device plugin to stop returning "no decision".  Kubelet has a bit of logic which says when to start nuking runtime containers that aren't needed (handlepodcleanups is not run until all pods have been admitted at least once), which may need to be tweaked slightly.

> Is this going to be an opt-in capability at a pod level or a node level?

I don't think so.  An admission plugin simply says "i can't admit this yet", and the kubelet therefore keeps it in pending, and keeps retrying (eventually we have to put a message on the pod that says "we're still trying").  Alternatively, we could admit the pod and then simply add a soft lifecycle handler (it "looks" like this pod should run, but we can't be sure, so we'll simply defer taking action on it).  I'm not certain that's better though.

EDIT: There is an implicit assumption in admission that all decisions are fast, so device plugins should also be fast to initialize (and have low dependency fan out off the node).  Is that actually true?

> Perhaps decoupling admission and allocation could ease some of the pain here? I wonder what was the reason for coupling the two in the first place.

Yes but it's a big chunk of work.  I would say we didn't invest enough to define a durable mechanism that multiple plugins could use effectively.  There are a couple of bugs on it - https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/107074 is an example of the kind of problem that is hard to fix correctly today without it.

> Once all device plugins have checked in, i think it's reasonable for the device plugin to stop returning "no decision".

"All" here meaning all we know from the checkpoint file that the running pod we are currently re-admitting requires, right?

Anyway, I think we need a timeout too, because a device plugin might have crashed while kubelet was down and can be in a crash-loop or just plain gone. The pod might have to be killed eventually to give k8s a chance to schedule it elsewhere.

As I read the comments, a proper solution here may be non-trivial to implement and require more time for additional discussions. Would it make sense then to revert the breaking change meanwhile and work on a fix independently?

> As I read the comments, a proper solution here may be non-trivial to implement and require more time for additional discussions. Would it make sense then to revert the breaking change meanwhile and work on a fix independently?

@vasiliy-ul We are brainstorming possible options and are working towards a fix for this issue. Reverting the PR would mean we would have to reopen https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/109595 which is a valid issue and is impacting users as well.

In addition to that, we are just past the patch release cherry-pick deadline so reverts are not going to make their way into the impacted versions until next set of patch releases for at least another month.

Given that we HAVE to wait, it is probably best to aim for a fix. Also, given the critical nature of this bug and the timing, I think the first option recommended by @smarterclayton: `Making device manager intelligent and allowing admission of pods that were previously admitted (or in running phase)` is the way to go as it solves the problem in a less invasive way as compared to option 2 which (is overall nicer in the long run but) might need additional rounds of design discussion and time we can't afford right now.

> > my concern is that will require the device manager to gain knowledge about running pods, asking the pod cache or the kuberuntime
> 
> At admission time on a restart you won't actually know whether the pod is running, because the kubelet itself won't know, because admission on restart is the transition from "unknown state" to "should still be running". And the kubelet implemention is very naive - we assume admission is fast, reentrant, and cheap, none of which are completely true with the more complex admission requirements of cpu manager, device manager, etc.

Answering also your question below in the thread, AFAIK the admission (including resource allocation) is _usually_ fast and cheap enough, [but we may be quite vulnerable to failures](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/117435).

> I _think_ asking pod cache or kuberuntime directly would not be appropriate. However, at admission time you _do_ know what other pods have been previously admitted (passed as an argument), and you also know what pods _you've_ seen. So if you see a Running pod submitted to admission, and the device plugin internal state does not say that the pod's devices, you can treat that as "i previously admitted this" and accept it. If that requires significant changes to device manager internal state, it might be worth discussing what other changes to device manager might make sense.

I want to follow your guidelines here, but there's something I'm missing when implementing. I'm still wrapping my head around this area, there are flows I'm not quite familiar with.

A key part here is that I don't get yet from where the information about Running should come from. Should we just trust the information we get from the Pod(s) being passed to the admission, so, in practical terms, the Status of the pod being admitted? If so, however, we will need some extra care to distinguish node reboot vs kubelet restart.

- on kubelet restart we can assume the pod is running and don't allocate on admission
- on node reboot (which implies a kubelet restart) we should not and the current behavior to fail admission until plugins checked in seems still the best and correct

I pushed another draft PR to illustrate a possible solution. I'm leveraging [the fact the current code already queries the runtime.](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.25.0/pkg/kubelet/cm/container_manager_linux.go#L562)

I'm implementing this approach ("Impart device manager the intelligence so that it maintains an internal state of the pods that were previously admitted by it and take that into consideration when running pods are re-admitted on kubelet restarts.") because seems more self contained and easier to backport.
/cc
I plan to backport https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/118635 soon, starting with 1.27 and then down to 1.25 (included).
I want to add that this also happens when the node is rebooted. Running GPU pods are suddenly in `UnexpectedAdmissionError` because the nvidia device plugin is not ready yet.

> I want to add that this also happens when the node is rebooted. Running GPU pods are suddenly in `UnexpectedAdmissionError` because the nvidia device plugin is not ready yet.

yes, we're discussing improvements in #123980 and #124345

nodes.title: kubelet: devices: skip allocation for running pods
nodes.body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug
/kind regression

#### What this PR does / why we need it:
When kubelet initializes, runs admission for pods and possibly allocate requested resources. We need to distinguish between node reboot (no containers running) versus kubelet restart (containers potentially running).

Running pods should always survive kubelet restart. This means that device allocation on admission should not be attempted, because if a container requires devices and is still running when kubelet is restarting, that container already has devices allocated and working.
    
Thus, we need to properly detect this scenario in the allocation step and handle it explicitely. We need to inform the devicemanager about which pods are already running.

#### Which issue(s) this PR fixes:
Fixes #118559

#### Special notes for your reviewer:
Implements the first approach [proposed](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/118559#issuecomment-1584636260) in [the thread](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/118559#issuecomment-1584802420), so we make the devicemanager treat running pod differently.

This approach was chosen because it seems simpler to make self-contained and easier to backport.

The devicemanager already tracks (with the help of the checkpoint files) which containers got devices assigned to them, which by definition means these containers passed its admission. The missing bit is safely learning which container are already running when initializing, and for that we extend the [existing `buildContainerMapFromRuntime`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.28.0-alpha.2/pkg/kubelet/cm/container_manager_linux.go#L567)

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?
```release-note
Fixes regression causing running pods with devices to be terminated if kubelet is restarted
```

> Error should be either logged or, better event should be recorded, so user would see it in the kubelet describe pod output.

Logging is not enough, users don't have access to kubelet logs. Let's generate an event.

+1 on a condition.

From https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/118209#issuecomment-1577138274:
> FYI on the topic of conditions: https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-node/3085-pod-conditions-for-starting-completition-of-sandbox-creation. I suggest you sync with the authors of the KEP.
In https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/4063 I am proposing `ResourceClaimsReady` as new pod condition.

/triage accepted
/priority important-soon

Is it a bug or a feature? Will it be tracked as a part of the enhancement work? If so we can close this one
/cc
/cc

> Is it a bug or a feature?

Depends on expectations :sweat_smile: 

The [KEP says](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-node/3063-dynamic-resource-allocation#managing-resources): `Instead, a suitable event must be emitted which explains the problem`.

I expected this to be done already as part of the initial implementation, which would make this a bug. But one can also argue that this particular part had been deferred until later, which makes this a feature.

> Will it be tracked as a part of the enhancement work? If so we can close this one

We are using separate issues to track individual aspects of the enhancement work, so let's keep this open.

> Can you explain why do you prefer a condition over an event?

Let's focus on adding the event in this issue and discuss the condition in https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/4063#discussion_r1221066242

title: kubelet (1.27.1) fails to mount a hostPath volume for a static pod
body:
### What happened?

This is a bit hard to reproduce, as it happens in a very specific setup, the problems only happens with `kubelet` 1.27.1, downgrading to 1.26.4 fixes the problem.

In a single-node cluster controlplane pods run as static pods, Rook/Ceph is deployed, and some PVs/PVCs backed by Ceph.

After a unclean shutdown related to some PVs backed by Ceph not being unmounted (this is not a Kubernetes), the `kubelet` which comes up after a reboot doesn't start controlplane static pods, which essentially blocks every other pod from starting (as API server is done).

After a reboot, kubelet is running, but it keeps reporting an error about static pods like:

```
172.20.0.2: {"ts":1683110056228.5916,"caller":"kubelet/kubelet.go:1875","msg":"Unable to attach or mount volumes for pod; skipping pod","pod":{"name":"kube-apiserver-talos-default-controlplane-1","namespace":"kube-system"},"err":"unmounted volumes=[audit secrets config], unattached volumes=[], failed to process volumes=[]: timed out waiting for the condition"}
```

All of the volumes are `hostPath` volumes in a static pod:

```yaml
        volumes:
            - hostPath:
                path: /system/secrets/kubernetes/kube-apiserver
              name: secrets
            - hostPath:
                path: /system/config/kubernetes/kube-apiserver
              name: config
            - hostPath:
                path: /var/log/audit/kube
              name: audit
```

The kubelet is stuck in this state "forever", I tested at least for 8 hours.

If I downgrade the kubelet (without machine reboot) to 1.26.4, it immediately starts the static pods bringing up the node online.

If I try same scenario with reboot with kubelet 1.26.4, the problem doesn't occur either.



### What did you expect to happen?

Kubelet should run static pods after a reboot.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

It's a bit complicated set of workloads, but it's 100% reproducible. I could provide more logs if needed.

### Anything else we need to know?

/sig node

I did some bisecting, and it turns out the breaking change was introduced between versions:

```
Kubernetes v1.27.0-alpha.3.180+2c8f63f693d750 -- BROKEN
Kubernetes v1.27.0-alpha.3.178+0e9ad242bd32f1 -- WORKS

Found a reasonably simple reproducer:

1. Run a cluster with a pod that uses a CSI volume (`rook-ceph.rbd.csi.ceph.com` in this report, `csi-driver-hostpath` in my lab).
2. Stop the API server + restart kubelet.

> Apparently, the CSI volume reconstruction tries to reach the API server, which is bad. Esp. if the API server is a static pod. Investigating further.

There might be also something with unclean shutdown in my case - CSI volume is not unmounted before reboot, so kubelet tries to reconstruct it (?), but this blocks static pods from startings.

`NewVolumeManagerReconstruction` features moved _some_ OS / mount related probing closer to kubelet startup, before it starts mounting volumes for new pods (incl. static pods). While all volume plugins do not need to access the API server at this point to "reconstruct" their volumes, subsequent processing *does* need it:


* [reconstructVolume](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/49649c89ea8fa0c7f81103f735b089ed5537aa37/pkg/kubelet/volumemanager/reconciler/reconstruct_common.go#L183) calls [FindAttachablePluginBySpec](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/49649c89ea8fa0c7f81103f735b089ed5537aa37/pkg/kubelet/volumemanager/reconciler/reconstruct_common.go#L233) that needs to know if a volume is attachable or not, and for CSI it means it needs to read `CSIDriver.AttachRequired` from CSIDriver informer. This code can be refactored relatively easily not to call FindAttachablePluginBySpec for CSI volumes.

* Similarly, [updateStatesNew](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/49649c89ea8fa0c7f81103f735b089ed5537aa37/pkg/kubelet/volumemanager/reconciler/reconstruct_new.go#L106) calls [MarkVolumeAsAttached](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/49649c89ea8fa0c7f81103f735b089ed5537aa37/pkg/kubelet/volumemanager/reconciler/reconstruct_new.go#LL108C1-L108C1) that needs to know if the volume is attachable using the same informer. This looks harder to fix, it really needs to know if the volume is attachable or not.

When the API server is not available, kubelet waits indefinitely for the informer to sync.

nodes.title: Fix reconstruction of CSI volumes
nodes.body:
#### What type of PR is this?
/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:
During CSI volume reconstruction it's not possible to tell, if the volume is attachable or not - CSIDriver instance may not be available, because kubelet may not have connection to the API server at that time.
 
Therefore remove all calls to `FindAttachablePluginBySpec` here:

* Reorder `reconstructVolume` not to call `FindAttachablePluginBySpec` for CSI volumes. It's just a simple refactoring.
* Add *uncertain attach-abilty* state during reconstruction, so volume reconstruction can finish without an API server.  When the API server becomes available, then set attach-ability based on CSIDriver instances and allow unmounting of volumes.

title: Mismatched URLs for service-account-issuer-discovery and Open API Spec's swagger.json
body:
### What happened?

When I use the official Kubernetes Java Client (version 18.0.0) from within a pod using `Config.defaultClient()` to build an `ApiClient` and then access `getServiceAccountIssuerOpenIDConfiguration` in the `WellKnownApi` I get the following error:

```json
{
  "kind": "Status",
  "apiVersion": "v1",
  "metadata": {},
  "status": "Failure",
  "message": "forbidden: User \"system:serviceaccount:test:user\" cannot get path \"/.well-known/openid-configuration/\"",
  "reason": "Forbidden",
  "details": {},
  "code": 403
}
```

The same happens with the `OpenidApi#getServiceAccountIssuerOpenIDKeyset`.

However, the problem does not happen when I call the `/.well-known/openid-configuration` endpoint using the pod's service account and curl.

The problem is that the generated Open API spec indicates that the client should call `/.well-known/openid-configuration/` instead of `/.well-known/openid-configuration` (and similarly `/openid/v1/jwks/` instead of `/openid/v1/jwks`). While the API Server seems to resolve these endpoints just fine, the `ClusterRole` defined in the code does not have the trailing slashes and therefore rejects the requests with a 403:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/6a75e7c40cab5a0d96d815c3aa976dc98b4b0972/plugin/pkg/auth/authorizer/rbac/bootstrappolicy/policy.go#L521-L530

### What did you expect to happen?

I expected to be able to access these APIs from within a pod that has a mounted service account because this [documentation](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/configure-service-account/#service-account-issuer-discovery) suggests all that is required is a service account and because all clusters get this `ClusterRoleBinding` and this `ClusterRole` by default:

```yaml
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRoleBinding
metadata:
  annotations:
    rbac.authorization.kubernetes.io/autoupdate: "true"
  labels:
    kubernetes.io/bootstrapping: rbac-defaults
  name: system:service-account-issuer-discovery
roleRef:
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: ClusterRole
  name: system:service-account-issuer-discovery
subjects:
- apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: Group
  name: system:serviceaccounts
```

```yaml
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRole
metadata:
  annotations:
    rbac.authorization.kubernetes.io/autoupdate: "true"
  labels:
    kubernetes.io/bootstrapping: rbac-defaults
  name: system:service-account-issuer-discovery
rules:
- nonResourceURLs:
  - /.well-known/openid-configuration
  - /openid/v1/jwks
  verbs:
  - get
```

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Here is the Java snippet to reproduce it:

```Java
        ApiClient k8sApiClient = Config.fromCluster();
        WellKnownApi wellKnownApi = new WellKnownApi(k8sApiClient);
        try {
            wellKnownApi.getServiceAccountIssuerOpenIDConfiguration();
        } catch (ApiException e) {
            LOG.error("Message: " + e.getMessage() + " Response body: " + e.getResponseBody());
        }
```

When run from within a pod that has a service account mounted into it, the above code will fail.

You can also reproduce the error without the Java Client by running `curl --cacert /run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/ca.crt -H "Authorization: Bearer $(cat /run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token)"  https://kubernetes.default.svc/.well-known/openid-configuration/` from within a pod.

I can resolve the issue by updating the `system:service-account-issuer-discovery` cluster role to have the endpoints with the trailing `/`.

```yaml
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRole
metadata:
  annotations:
    rbac.authorization.kubernetes.io/autoupdate: "true"
  labels:
    kubernetes.io/bootstrapping: rbac-defaults
  name: system:service-account-issuer-discovery
rules:
- nonResourceURLs:
  - /.well-known/openid-configuration/
  - /.well-known/openid-configuration
  - /openid/v1/jwks/
  - /openid/v1/jwks
  verbs:
  - get
```

### Anything else we need to know?

I am happy to provide a fix, if I can get the right pointers. The detail I'm unclear on is how to fix this in a backwards compatible way.

Also, this PR seems to have introduced the potentially problematic `swagger.json` entry: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/93258.

### Kubernetes version

<details>

Here is one of the remote clusters I reproduced the issues with.

```console
$ kubectl version
 kubectl version
Client Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"25", GitVersion:"v1.25.3", GitCommit:"434bfd82814af038ad94d62ebe59b133fcb50506", GitTreeState:"clean", BuildDate:"2022-10-12T10:47:25Z", GoVersion:"go1.19.2", Compiler:"gc", Platform:"darwin/amd64"}
Kustomize Version: v4.5.7
Server Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"23", GitVersion:"v1.23.2", GitCommit:"9d142434e3af351a628bffee3939e64c681afa4d", GitTreeState:"clean", BuildDate:"2022-01-19T17:29:16Z", GoVersion:"go1.17.5", Compiler:"gc", Platform:"linux/amd64"}
WARNING: version difference between client (1.25) and server (1.23) exceeds the supported minor version skew of +/-1
```

</details>


### Cloud provider

I reproduced this bug in multiple cloud providers as well as in minikube. It does not appear to be cloud provider specific.

title: StatefulSet with `podManagementPolicy: Parallel` should create pods in parallel
body:
### What would you like to be added?

When `podManagementPolicy: Parallel` is set, StatefulSetController should issue create requests for replicas in batches (similar to how other controllers work, e.g. ReplicaSetController) when creating pods for the first time and scaling up.

### Why is this needed?

Currently even with `Parallel` podManagementPolicy StatefulSet the replicas are still _created_ sequentially, even though they can start to _run_ in any order.

This severely limits pod throughput when working with large StatefulSets (~thousands of replicas). For example, 10 StatefulSets with 5k pods each achieve a total of ~6 pods/s, while 1k StatefulSets with 50 pods each allows for creating ~120 pods/s. 

`Parallel` policy suggests the pods can be created sequentially (https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/kubernetes-api/workload-resources/stateful-set-v1/#StatefulSetSpec): 

>The alternative policy is Parallel which will create pods in parallel to match the desired scale without waiting, and on scale down will delete all pods at once.

Relevant code (`Parallel` policy controls the value of `monotonic`): https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/statefulset/stateful_set_control.go#L424)

title: Jobs create replacement Pods as soon as a Pod is marked for deletion
body:
### What happened?

When a Pod belonging to a Job is deleted, the job controller creates a replacement pod immediately, even if parallelism is set to 1 and backoffLimit is set to 0.

### What did you expect to happen?

This depends on the use case, but some applications fail when there are more than one pod.

For example, tensorflow fails with:

```
 /job:worker/task:4: Duplicate task registration with task_name=/job:worker/replica:0/task:4
```

This applications will benefit from a delayed Pod creation until the original Pod is marked as Failed/Succeeded.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create a Job that takes some time to clean up on SIGTERM. You can use `gcr.io/k8s-staging-perf-tests/sleep` with `-termination-grace-period 1m`
2. Delete the pod.
3. Observe that there are two pods running.

While here we do a manual DELETE, it could come as a result of preemption from kube-scheduler or a Node maintenance event, which could be common.

### Anything else we need to know?

IIUC, the existing behavior is similar to that of ReplicaSets and it's the behavior that Jobs had from the beginning.

A comment from an internal discussion with @erictune:

> This non-locking behavior was chosen when Job was designed.  At that time, there was no completionMode: Indexed.  Without an index, even if we waited for complete termination, the user would still need to do their own locking/coordination process, or ensure idempotence.  So it would just slow down the Job controller with no benefit.  

Also, at that time there was no PodFailurePolicy. If the user sets a rule for FailJob, we might be creating a replacement pod before being able to act on the policy (related to point 3 in https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-apps/3329-retriable-and-non-retriable-failures#marking-pods-as-failed kubernetes/enhancements#3329).

So I propose that we treat this as a bugfix for Jobs (Indexed or NonIndexed) that use the PodFailurePolicy (still in Beta).

While an argument could be made that this is an issue with Indexed Jobs, regardless of whether they are using PodFailurePolicy, it's unclear if there are users depending on fast recreation. We could provide this as an option in the PodFailurePolicy as well.

> I don't have capacity to work on this for 1.27 and TBH, it's probably good to have a KEP just for this. I'll come back to this in the next release, unless anybody else wants to take a stab.

A new KEP implies having to work on this for 1.28 or later.

> Point 3 seems contingent on https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/115331 so I'm not sure if we can implement this now?

That is a very good point against doing this in 1.27. Old kubelets that don't mark pods as Failed can hold the progress of a Job. But we should be good to have the new feature as beta in 1.29 (because we support n-2 kubelets)

> That is a very good point against doing this in 1.27. Old kubelets that don't mark pods as Failed can hold the progress of a Job. But we should be good to have the new feature as beta in 1.29 (because we support n-2 kubelets)

@kannon92 @alculquicondor As PR #115331 lands in 1.27 it unblocks the work in this feature for 1.28.

1. outside of `podFailurePolicy`, new KEP
**Pro**: allows to transfer the semantics to workloads which don't have `podFailurePolicy`
**Pro**: would not delay pod failure policy graduation
**Con**: is coupled to pod failure policy graduation

2. under `podFailurePolicy`, new KEP
**Pro**: would not delay pod failure policy graduation

3. under `podFailurePolicy`, under the existing KEP
**Pro**: coupling to the feature reflects the status quo
**Pro**: coupling to pod failure policy can give better impact to the feature
**Con**: may delay graduation of pod failure policy

pending discussion on sig apps of course

title: Volumes cannot be expanded with out-of-tree CSI drivers
body:
### What happened?

I was trying to add volume expansion support to an out-of-tree CSI driver (https://github.com/apalia/cloudstack-csi-driver), then when I actually tried to expand a volume which I had created, I saw an error message from kube-controller-manager saying "didn't find a plugin capable of expanding the volume; waiting for an external controller to process this PVC".
After some debugging, I found that the `ProbeExpandableVolumePlugins` function in app/plugins.go does not call `csi.ProbeVolumePlugins()`, like the `ProbeAttachableVolumePlugins` function does. Instead, it creates a list of legacy volume plugins and a few hard-coded ones, but CSI is missing from that list:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/c2a7bfd6b4f147b40c3b2132aae003ff21a142bb/cmd/kube-controller-manager/app/plugins.go#L73
Later on, when trying to expand a volume, the `FindPluginBySpec` function in volume/plugins.go will return the error "no volume plugin matched" because CSI is not in its list of plugins.

Was CSI intentionally omitted? The [CSI developer documentation](https://kubernetes-csi.github.io/docs/volume-expansion.html) says that CSI drivers can implement volume expansion, so it seems odd that `ProbeExpandableVolumePlugins` does not include CSI in its list.

### What did you expect to happen?

I expected volumes to be expandable with out-of-tree CSI drivers.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Any out-of-tree CSI driver should do, but I have a fork of the CloudStack CSI driver to which I'm trying to add volume expansion support: https://github.com/maxerenberg/cloudstack-csi-driver

Follow the instructions in the README to deploy a new CSI driver (set allowVolumeExpansion to true when deploying the StorageClass), then create a PersistentVolumeClaim, attach it to a pod, and try to expand it.

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

### Kubernetes version

<details>

```console
$ kubectl version

title: `kubectl expose` fails for apps with same-port, different-protocol
body:
Given this deployment:

```
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: multiport
spec:
  replicas: 0
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: multiport
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: multiport
    spec:
      containers:
      - image: k8s.gcr.io/serve_hostname:v1.4
        name: c1
        ports:
        - containerPort: 93
          protocol: TCP
        - containerPort: 93
          protocol: UDP
```

```
$ k expose deploy multiport
The Service "multiport" is invalid: spec.ports[1]: Duplicate value: core.ServicePort{Name:"", Protocol:"UDP", AppProtocol:(*string)(nil), Port:93, TargetPort:intstr.IntOrString{Type:0, IntVal:0, StrVal:""}, NodePort:0}
```

Looking at staging/src/k8s.io/kubectl/pkg/cmd/expose/expose.go, it builds a `protocolsMap` which reduces those 2 ports to one protocol.  It should probably just return a list of {proto, port} or even {proto, port, name} which it extracts from the target.

nodes.body: /triage accepted
interesting, we have all this multi-port same number and different protocol problem in a lot of places 🤔

I think it's failing because `kubectl expose` doesn't supports that system. In K8s, specifying multiple ports with the same port number but different protocols is not allowed. Try using `kubectl create service` intead of expose, it will allow you to specify multiple ports with the same port number but different protocols, using the --tcp and --udp flags.
I'd like to work on this, if that's a valid use-case :)

> I'd like to work on this, if that's a valid use-case :)

/assign @anggao 

you have a reproducer in the description, it will need a test to reproduce the issue, it seems that there are no unit tests for deployments https://github.com/kubernetes/kubectl/blob/master/pkg/cmd/expose/expose_test.go
@adityassharma-ss - the problem is that `expose` tries to do it and then fails.  I didn't even know we would try until someone raised this issue with me.  I had to go try it to be sure.
Yes! I'd like to work on this case.

Agreed with @thockin, it looks like the problem is in [expose.go](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/530f65d6fd5af81c0691143fbf2c00d440476bb9/staging/src/k8s.io/kubectl/pkg/cmd/expose/expose.go#L422-L454)
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/530f65d6fd5af81c0691143fbf2c00d440476bb9/staging/src/k8s.io/kubectl/pkg/cmd/expose/expose.go#L445-L447

And stems from how it gets the [ports](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/9f3384f02f472b0095fe3675139c08e7aaa7e711/staging/src/k8s.io/kubectl/pkg/polymorphichelpers/portsforobject.go#L62-L78) and [protocols](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/9f3384f02f472b0095fe3675139c08e7aaa7e711/staging/src/k8s.io/kubectl/pkg/polymorphichelpers/protocolsforobject.go#L64-L89) separately from each other, and then tries to match them back together when creating the service.  The map key is the port number, so it (the code in expose.go) doesn't allow for the same port to have multiple protocols.

As Tim said, returning them together should allow this to be fixed.

title: Scheduling Pods with dynamic resources and using the Pod `.spec.nodeName` field fails
body:
### What happened?

The combination of using the Pod spec nodeName field with the `DynamicResources` scheduler plugin (currently feature-gated) doesn't work. No surprise really as the nodeName field effective bypasses the `DynamicResources` scheduler plugin running, and something rather clever would need to be invented to make things to work. But this is still a bit of a regression compared to the old device plugin model which doesn't have a similar limitation.  @pohly as the author of the dynamic resources feature can explain what could maybe be created to fix this.

Granted, forcing scheduling even with a device plugin resource may or may not succeed at the node level depending on the availability of said plugin resources at the node, but with dynamic resources the failure seems to be currently guaranteed.

The use-case for this is such that the Kubernetes scheduler is effectively being preceded by some other scheduler which runs earlier (say, some HPC framework) which is giving the Pods the node names and somehow knows that there will be enough resources, and then the workloads ought to land in the specified node and the container related work is then handled normally from there on. So basically Kubernetes wouldn't do much in terms of scheduling, but takes over from there.

### What did you expect to happen?

TBH I expected it to fail and it did. The resource claims won't work, since the scheduler plugin isn't getting a chance to do its thing.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Just use DRA with Pod spec nodeName field, one needs a DRA driver obviously.

### Anything else we need to know?

One possible solution would be to have a new controller which specifically watches for pods in this state (nodeName set and reference claims). That controller then must trigger delayed allocation (if needed) by creating a PodScheduling object with selectedNode set. After allocation it must add the pod to the reservedFor list.

kubelet will immediately try to run the pod once it sees it because of the nodeName field. It will refuse to run it until eventually all claims are allocated and reserved.

Obviously using a scheduler which is not aware of dynamic resources is problematic. There is no guarantee that the chosen node even has the hardware that is needed for the pod and that it isn't in use. It would be good to hear from whoever has this use case whether the solution outlined above would work in practice.

The alternative is to build support for dynamic resource allocation into that other scheduler.

nodes.title: dra: pre-scheduled pods
nodes.body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind feature

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

When someone decides that a Pod should definitely run on a specific node, they
can create the Pod with spec.nodeName already set. Some custom scheduler might
do that. Then kubelet starts to check the pod and (if DRA is enabled) will
refuse to run it, either because the claims are still waiting for the first
consumer or the pod wasn't added to reservedFor. Both are things the scheduler
normally does.
    
Also, if a pod got scheduled while the DRA feature was off in the
kube-scheduler, a pod can reach the same state.
    
#### Which issue(s) this PR fixes:
Fixes https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/114005

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

The resource claim controller can handle these two cases by taking over for the
kube-scheduler when nodeName is set. Triggering an allocation is simpler than
in the scheduler because all it takes is creating the right
PodSchedulingContext with spec.selectedNode set. There's no need to list nodes
because that choice was already made, permanently. Adding the pod to
reservedFor also isn't hard.
    
What's currently missing is triggering de-allocation of claims to re-allocate
them for the desired node. This is not important for claims that get created
for the pod from a template and then only get used once, but it might be
worthwhile to add de-allocation in the future.


#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?
```release-note
kube-controller-manager: the dynamic resource controller steps in when a pod got created such that the scheduler ignores it (i.e. spec.nodeName is set) and then takes care of triggering delayed resource claim allocation and/or reserving a claim for the pod.
```

#### Additional documentation e.g., KEPs (Kubernetes Enhancement Proposals), usage docs, etc.:

```docs
-KEP: https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/3063
```

``Detach`` should be called only after a volume was successfully unmounted by all nodes' Kubelet. 

In Kubelet a volume was unmounted only after the pod that uses the volume was deleted from Apiserver and made sure all container was stopped. Therefore A pod that existed in Apiserver which means unmount can't able to call.

I kindly request to reopen.

Non-graceful node shutdown does not address this problem. Non-graceful node shutdown aims to address a completely separate issue: if I know a node went down in an unexpected way, how do I manualy tell `k8s` that I know the node is down and resources like `VolumeAttachments` and `Pods` can be force-deleted safely because I am sure they are not active on the dead node.

The problem at least I see here regards what should happen automatically. As of version `v1.32.2` after the 6-minute timer for forced detach expires, contrary to expectations, nothing happens as forced detach will only occur if the related pod is no longer running. This however will not be the case if a node goes down unexpectedly as the pod will be then stuck terminating. 

What I, and from my knowledge many other users, would expect to happen is for pods on nodes that have been `NotReady` for some time to be force-terminated automatically to allow rescheduling. Obviously many workloads cannot allow such a behavior as has been explained a countless number of times in this bug tracker. However, many also require it and it would be nice to see an upstream option to enable such a behavior, given that most of the required code is already in place (it would basically be automatic non-graceful node shutdown after a period of time).

Judging from the fact that a large commercial CSI provider like Longhorn backed by an enormous company like SUSE has decided to implement (such a feature)[https://longhorn.io/docs/1.9.1/high-availability/node-failure/] and has been supporting it for years, there is most definitely a use case for such a behavior.

I know this looks like a perfect use case for an operator, however, to my knowledge, as of today, there is no widely-adopted one which leads to many vendors developing in-house solutions for this problem. Again, it would be nice to see an upstream solution to such a common problem as it has been requested a countless number of times. Many users simply need the option to force-terminate pods on nodes that are down for a longer period of time.

The argument that it could lead to data loss no longer holds with non-graceful node shutdown in place. Non-graceful node shutdown also could but we have the option to tell `k8s` that we know what we are doing and the node is surely down. It would only be logical to also allow users to tell `k8s` that we know what we are doing and please force-terminate pods on nodes that have been down for a specified amount of time. It would be nice if `kubelet` did the same on its side if `apiserver` cannot be contacted for a specified interval and those two optional features would nicely complement each other as not all workloads are cloud-native and clustered. In fact, most aren't and even some of those that are could take advantage of not having to manually clean up `StatefulSet` pods if a node goes down in an unexpected way.

If this should be moved into a separate issue let me know

title: WaitForAttachAndMount might delay pod terminating.
body:
From comment https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/100047#issuecomment-796980046

syncPod is waiting for volumes to finish mounting. before calling WaitForAttachAndMount, it checks if the pod is terminated before entering. However, if the pod is terminated after that check, then we are stuck in in WaitForAttachAndMount until it times out, a little over 2 minutes.

The call probably needs to be enhanced to return early if the pod is deleted. It doesn't seem like pod deletion is captured as a pod error. In fact, we seem to pop all errors if the pod is deleted.

cc @Random-Liu

found similar issue and PR to address it https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/49663
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/49724

In syncPod workflow, there are three places checking whether pod is terminated 

1. if pod is not runnable, or deletionTimeStamp is set, or pod is failed, trigger killPod() and return
 [code link](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go#L1590)

2. if pod is not termniated (!kl.podIsTerminated(pod) ), do not create cgroup etc.
 [code link](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go#L1617) 

3. if pod is not termniated (!kl.podIsTerminated(pod) ), do not wait for volume mounts
[code link](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go#L1698)

So in case during one particular syncPod, two cases

- pod deletion timestamp is not set yet, then pod is considered not terminated, syncPod will waitForAttachMount(). If at this point, volume is actually unmounted (or will not mount at all because volume is already removed from desired state)
- pod deletion timestamp is set already, syncPod will return immediately at first check shown above. 

So my thought is #49724 is actually does not help on problem #49663. Two possible proposals here to help this
1. reduce waitForAttachandMount timeout (e.g., 2mins-1min). Concern is not sure how it will affect performance for normal pod startup
2. waitForAttachandMount only checks actual state, it is possible to also check desired state. If the volume is no longer in desired state, should stop and return immediately. 

@msau42 @Random-Liu, any thoughts?
I prefer option 2 so that it exits the wait faster in error conditions and doesn't impact the normal case.
cc @mauriciopoppe

now I tried to implement this logic and realized for option 2, we cannot differentiate whether pod volume is removed from desired state or it is not yet added to the state. In many cases, it might not yet added to desired state, then we return error immediately, which might affect the performance..

A third option is to make sure while pod is still in sync phase by pod worker, make sure volume is not removed from desired state so that volume will go through attach and mount normally. But this might also slow down pod deletion in case volumes take more time to attach and mount..
if it's not added yet to desired state, then we will return error from the call. Are you concerned that syncPod will take too long to retry?

> if it's not added yet to desired state, then we will return error from the call. Are you concerned that syncPod will take too long to retry?

right. I remember if there is no pod update event happened, pod worker sync up pod after a period of time.
Is there some other state we can check? To make it this far in `syncPod`, are there any assumptions we can make?
